definition: Heavy aggressive volume meeting resting orders at a price and failing to move price through it: sellers hitting bids that hold, or buyers lifting offers that hold. It lasts only while price holds. If price moves through and stays beyond, the read becomes acceptance.

Price building time and volume at a new price instead of passing through it. Acceptance moves value; a quick visit does not. The mechanical acceptance test this course uses at a level is taught in Module 10.
How far price went against a trade or an occurrence before it ended, measured from the entry price, as a positive number of ticks. The journal records it as mae_ticks on every trade.

The order-flow confirmation in this course: the side pushing into a named level is running out. It is recorded with one of four sub-forms (big-orders, failing-delta, delta-divergence, two-bar-exhaustion) on every trade that uses it. It is never a trigger; a price event must also fire.

The average of the true range over a set number of bars, commonly 14. True range is the largest of: the bar's high minus its low, the high minus the prior close, and the prior close minus the low. It describes how far price usually travels in a bar; it says nothing about direction.
An auction rotating around an agreed price, inside edges both sides defend. Value areas overlap from one session to the next. The profile is wide in the middle and thin at the edges.

The fixed amount you risk on a full-size trade, chosen once from your account and the losing run you can sit through. Every result is measured in it. It does not rise after a good week or fall after a bad one; it changes only at a scheduled review, written as a new line on the page.

How often an outcome happened across every case in a closed, dated data set, with no condition applied: the count of cases where it happened divided by the count of cases. It describes that set. It is not a forecast for the next session.
The big-orders sub-form: passive size that holds and prints at the level. Aggressors keep hitting it and price does not get through.
Breathing in four equal counts: in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four. One round is all four sides of the box.

One conditional line of the plan: a level, the behaviour and trigger that switch it on, the target, the invalidation that ends it, and a conviction. On the Module 16 sheet each branch is written as one Idea line.
The journal tag for breaking a hard rule: an entry outside the trading window, a position held through a Tier One release, a stop widened after entry, or trading past the kill switch.
A label for an entry in your own register: the rule beats its null and is stable across both halves, every year and the recent stretch, but has not yet met the thresholds of both gates.

An event that brings participants to the market at a known or sudden time, such as a Tier One release, a Fed decision or an unscheduled headline. In idea generation it sets the clock and can print new levels; it never sets a direction.

A written pass over the day's chart, level by level: what price did at each marked level, what you did there, and, for every trade you exited, whether price reached the planned target after your exit.

The same count taken only over the cases that meet a stated condition, such as where the session opened. It always carries its condition and its own, smaller sample size, and it is only usable if the condition can be checked at the moment you would use the number.

The range of true rates that could plausibly have produced the count you observed, at a stated confidence (usually 95%). It is how wide the error around a rate is. It narrows as n grows, roughly with the square root of n: four times the sample, half the width.

The arithmetic that turns three answered questions into an order, always in this order: the level (the zone traded against and the target level), the stop (behind the far edge), the risk (the stop distance, and the 2:1 check to the target), the size (from the stop distance and the grade), and the entry. It comes after the three tiers, never before them.
The fixed dollar amount the exchange multiplies the index by to value one contract. For MNQ it is $2 per index point; for MES it is $5. It is also the contract's point value.

A label of strong, moderate or thin attached to one branch: how much structure and context stand behind its thesis. It is recorded for the journal. It doesn't change your size and it isn't a direction.

The running total of bar delta from the start of the session. It shows which side has been more aggressive over the day. It is slow, can stay positive through a fall, and is context for the session, never a signal on its own.
Your loss limit for the day: 2R. Reaching it fires the kill switch. Not the same as a prop firm's Max Loss Limit (MLL), which is an account-level drawdown set by the firm.

The futures or stock a market maker holds against an options book so that small price moves leave it roughly flat. As price moves, the hedge the book needs changes, and the dealer must trade to keep up: forced flow that is set by the options book, not by any view on direction.

In the current session, the low of a pullback in a move up (or the high of a pullback in a move down) after which price went on beyond the swing extreme that came before the pullback. It stays a level until price trades back through it.

In footprint charts, delta is the difference between buying volume (contracts traded at the ask) and selling volume (contracts traded at the bid). Positive delta means more buying; negative delta means more selling. It reveals the aggression behind a move.
The delta-divergence sub-form: price makes a new extreme on approach to the level and delta does not. Read on the approach, not on arrival.
The current session's VPOC and value edges as its profile builds. They move as volume builds, so each is used at the price it shows when your trigger fires, and that price is the one you record.

A footprint cell flagged because aggressive volume on one side outweighs the other side diagonally: buying at a price against selling one tick below it, or selling at a price against buying one tick above it, by at least a set ratio and a set minimum difference in contracts. Not the auction imbalance of Module 05.

The journal analysis rule that any cohort (a group of trades sharing a field such as setup or trigger) below 30 trades, or below 20 distinct sessions, is shown dimmed with a warning. Dimmed means visible but marked as not yet a sample. It is never hidden, and clearing the floor is a minimum for reading a cohort, not a verdict on it.

A moving average that weights recent prices more heavily. In this course a moving average is never a level: the 9 EMA pullback is a continuation-only entry trigger (Module 13), judged on a close, and a reclaim against the move is not that trigger.

The fixed routine run within an hour of the 16:00 ET close, on every trading day whatever the result: the chart mark-up, the post-exit fields and execution mark for every trade, and one line on the day.
The hours the futures trade outside RTH: from 16:00 ET until the daily halt, and from the reopen until 09:30 ET the next morning.
A tail of thin, quickly-traded prices at a session's high or low: price reached the extreme, found the other side waiting, and left fast. Excess marks an auction that finished at that end.

Pass or Fail, assigned after the exit: did the exit follow the plan? Pass is a target, the planned scale, a pre-set invalidation, the stop, or session end. Anything else is Fail. Kept separate from the grade so the grade never reads the outcome.

How you acted on the plan: whether the trigger fired before entry, the stop sat behind structure, the size matched the plan, and the exit followed it. It is graded by the grade rubric and the execution mark, never by the result.
The average result per trade in R: win % × average win − loss % × average loss. It is the one number that combines how often a rule wins with how much it wins and loses.
The failing-delta sub-form: delta declining on approach. Each bar coming into the level carries less aggression in the direction of the push than the one before.
The edge of a zone on the far side from where price arrives. For a level above current price it is the top of the zone; for a level below, the bottom. The stop goes behind it.

The plan as it stands at 09:25: one paragraph made of one sentence of context in location words, one sentence per branch, and one sentence for the nothing case. No day-type label, no directional call.

Three questions asked in order about any event or break. First order: what happened. Second order: who was already positioned for it. Third order: who is now forced to transact, and which way their exit pushes.
The urge to enter because price is moving without you. On this site it is a reason to check the plan: a trade with no named level and no trigger is No Setup, whatever price is doing.

An advanced chart type that shows the volume traded at each price level within each candle, split into buying volume (traded at the ask) and selling volume (traded at the bid). In this course it can confirm a trigger at a level; it is never the trigger.

Orders from a participant who must buy or sell regardless of price: a dealer re-hedging, a fund rebalancing to a rule, a margin call, a triggered stop. It changes how fast and how far price moves once it starts. It carries no information about where price should be.

A standardised exchange-traded contract to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date. Index futures are cash-settled and leveraged; Module 03 covers the contract, ticks, sessions, settlement and margin.

Whether dealers, in aggregate, are estimated to be net long options (their hedging leans against moves) or net short (their hedging goes with moves). It describes how price may move, never where or which way. In this course it may weight conviction only; it is never a location, a target or an if-clause.
An RTH open outside the prior day's range: above the PD High or below the PD Low. Nothing else is a gap in this course. The Gap Setups (Module 12) target the PD range edge, not the prior close.

The test of a locked rule on historical market data. It passes at n of at least 100 trades, beating a volatility-preserving null, positive in both halves and in each calendar year, plus a 2023–2026 recency check, reported in R with n, win %, expectancy and the null's expectancy.

The test of your own live trades of a rule. It passes at n of at least 30 live trades, across at least 20 distinct sessions, with expectancy of at least +0.3R after commissions. Sim trades never count toward it.

The electronic trading session for futures that runs outside regular market hours. For MNQ, Globex runs nearly 23 hours a day. The overnight high (ON High) and low (ON Low) from Globex are key levels marked before each regular session. In this course the hours outside RTH are called ETH.

The entry-plan score given to every trade at entry, before it resolves, from four checks: the location is a named level, the trigger fired before entry, the stop is behind structure, and the size matches the plan for that stop. A+ is all four with a fill within 2 ticks of the intended price; A is all four; B is three of four with no breach of the stop or size check; C is two or fewer, or any breach of those two. C is no trade.

A wide section of a profile, where a lot of volume traded over a range of prices. It is a balance inside the profile: both sides did business there, and price tends to slow down and rotate when it returns.

A conditional statement written before the session: a thesis in if/then form at a named level, the invalidation that ends it, and a conviction grade of strong, moderate or thin. It describes what you will do if price reaches a place, not where price will go.
An auction in which one side is in charge and price moves to find new business. Value migrates: each session's value area sits beyond the last one, with little or no overlap.
A level that forms during the current session, from one of the types on the in-session list. It counts only once it has finished forming, and only if your plan named its type before the session.
The deposit required to open a futures position, per contract. It is good-faith money held against what the position might lose, not a cost and not a cap on the loss.
The named price, judged on a candle close of a stated timeframe, at which a branch's thesis is wrong. It sits at or behind the zone's far edge. Written before the session, never moved during it.

Your daily max loss: 2R, twice your fixed base risk per trade. When the day's loss reaches it, trading stops until the next session. It is set at the account level so that it fires whether or not you agree with it.
A label for an entry in your own register: the rule failed its test. The entry keeps the reason it failed and a reopen condition, so it is never re-run blind and never stays dead by accident.

A sound-on alert set on a marked zone before the session. Each zone carries two: one at the edge price will reach first, which calls you to the screen, and one at the far edge, which tells you price has traded through the whole zone.

The daily trade a leveraged or inverse fund makes to restore its target multiple of an index's daily return. It buys after up days and sells after down days, in the direction the day already moved, and is concentrated toward the close.
An order to buy or sell at a specific price or better. A buy limit order fills at or below your price; a sell limit fills at or above. You control the price but not whether the order fills.
The account state after a loss limit fires: open positions are closed, working orders are cancelled, and only orders that reduce a position are accepted until the reset.
Where a trade happens: one named level from the pre-marked or in-session list, written as a zone, with the stop behind its far edge. It is recorded by its slug in the journal's location field.

A rule written in full, and dated, before the data that tests it is opened: rule, entry, stop, target and window in one paragraph, plus costs and the null. Any change after the data is seen is a new rule with a new register entry.
Buying a contract or asset with the expectation that price will rise. You profit when price goes up. The opposite of short.
A thin section of a profile, where little volume traded. Price moved through it quickly the first time; with no business to hold it, it tends to move through quickly again, toward the next HVN.
The lower level your account must stay above to keep the position open. Fall below it and you must add funds or the position is reduced or closed for you.
Closing a working position yourself, before its target or its resting stop has done it for you.

Your pre-session judgment of where the day's business can happen: the context, the levels that get branches, the room and the clock. After the session it is graded on one question: did price do at the level what a branch said it might, or did the nothing case hold?
The single written sentence that ends the trading day: trades taken, how many marked Pass, and that tomorrow starts from its own plan. It is the last step of the end-of-day routine.
The location tag for any price outside every zone on your list: no named level, so nothing for a stop to sit behind. It exists so that a trade taken there is counted rather than hidden.
A micro futures contract on the Nasdaq-100 index at one-tenth the size of NQ. Each point is worth $2 and each 0.25 tick $0.50. It is the illustration instrument for this course's worked examples.

A journal tag that records an emotion-driven or rule-breaking action on a trade, split into entry and exit: for example Impulsive, Too Early or Broke Rule. A trade built and exited to plan that lost carries none.
The journal tag for a trade with no named location and read behind it: a trade taken on feel. An idea without a written invalidation is No Setup, however good it sounds.
The line of the plan that names where no branch applies, written as a price range with two numbers, plus anything the plan has no branch for. In the nothing case the action is no trade.

The same locked rule run on price paths rebuilt from each session's own 1-minute returns, shuffled within 30-minute blocks. Shuffling destroys any real sequence while keeping the session's volatility. Its average expectancy across many shuffles is the baseline the rule must beat.
A name for how price behaved in the first minutes after the 09:30 open. It describes those minutes only. It is vocabulary, never a call for the rest of the day.
The high and low of the session from 09:30 ET to the end of a window you choose and write on your plan. They become levels, or-high and or-low, only once the window has closed.
The day each month when listed equity and index options expire. On the pre-market sheet it is written as a noun on the calendar line: context about activity for the session, never a direction.
A retired term. The opening range's high and low can be levels once the window closes; a breakout of the range is not a setup in this course. Module 24 covers how such ideas are tested.

The dated list in your PlayBook of ideas you are not trading: setups you saw elsewhere, variations, filters, new levels. An idea leaves the parking lot only at a scheduled review, and only into your register, never straight onto a page.

term: PD High / PD Low (Prior Day High/Low)
definition: The highest and lowest prices reached in yesterday's regular trading session. They are pre-marked levels, scoped to RTH: a location on the plan, not a call on which way price will go from it.
What you write before a session: one or more branches and a nothing case. It says what you will do at each place price can go. It never says where price will go.

Your own written book of trades: one page per setup you actually take, each with the same fixed fields, plus a parking lot for everything else. It describes what you do at a level, never where price will go.

One page of your PlayBook for one working-set line, filled in with the same nine fields every time: name, location, read, trigger, construction, invalidation, worked composite, status in your register, and last review date. A page with an empty field is a draft, not a page.

The single price with the most volume traded in the period: the price the session agreed on most. Built from volume it is the VPOC. The prior session's VPOC is the level PD VPOC. On your plan it is a location and a target, never a trigger.
What one full index point is worth on one contract, in dollars. It equals the multiplier: $2 for MNQ, $5 for MES. Point value is tick value divided by tick size.
A session extreme with no excess: price stopped flat, often at the same price in two or more 30-minute periods, and nothing traded beyond it. The auction stopped there without being refused.

The fixed routine run after every losing trade and before any new entry: a physical step to slow down, then three questions answered aloud. If you can't answer them clearly, you are not ready to trade.

A level built before the session from completed data and taken from one fixed list: the prior day, settlement, the overnight session, the prior week and the higher-timeframe profile. Each carries a session scope, and only these go on the pre-market sheet.

The one page you fill before every session: readiness score, context, news, levels as zones, the idea, the systems check, the rehearsal and the time you finished. Finished by 09:25 ET. A completed sheet clears you to trade; an incomplete one doesn't.

The name traders give to the quarterly expiry Friday in March, June, September and December, when the quarterly equity index futures expire (Module 03) on the same day as that month's options. Written on the calendar line as activity context, never as a direction.

The dollar amount risked on a single trade, based on your stop loss. If your stop is 10 ticks away and each tick is $0.50, your R = $5. The journal records every outcome in R (2R is twice the risk), so trades of different sizes compare on one scale.
A run of entries taken one after another without a fresh setup, usually starting after the session's first win: each trade comes faster and from further away from a level than the one before.

A 0 to 2 score written at the top of the pre-market sheet. 2: curious about what the market will do at your levels. 1: neutral. 0: needing something from the market today. It is recorded as data for the journal, not used as a gate.

Your own written list of trading ideas under test. Each entry carries a number, the locked rule paragraph, the date it was locked, its test results in R, its gate results, its label and, if it failed, the reason and a reopen condition.

One numbered, dated page in your own register for one idea: the rule as locked before any data was opened, the null it is tested against, its status, its n (live and sim shown apart), and its reopen condition if it failed. A change to the rule is a new entry, never an edit.

The label your own register gives one of your ideas, from your own tests. Untested: written, not yet run against data. Watch: positive but unstable, or too few occurrences. Candidate: the rule beats its null and is stable across both halves, every year and the recent stretch, but has not yet met the thresholds of both gates. Validated: passed both of your gates. Killed: failed, with its reason and reopen condition written. It describes your record of your idea, nothing else.

Running the written plan once, aloud, before the open: the idea at its level, the trigger, the stop, the stop filling, the post-loss reset and the kill switch. A practised step, the same every day, not a hope about the session.
The specific new evidence or new rule that would justify testing a failed idea again, written into its register entry at the moment it fails. A reopened idea is a new entry, tested from scratch.

Moving from the expiring contract month to the next one: your charts, your levels and any position you intend to keep. For US equity index futures the customary roll date is the Monday before the third-Friday expiry.

An oscillator from 0 to 100 that compares the size of recent up closes with recent down closes over a set number of bars, commonly 14. It describes how one-sided the recent run has been. In this course it is never a thesis, a trigger, an exit or a direction.

For equity index futures, 09:30 to 16:00 ET, the hours of the US cash equity session. Other contracts have their own regular session, listed on their CME spec page. In this course, prior-day levels and settlement are scoped to RTH.
The number of independent cases a rate was counted on. A rate means little without it, and every rate on a page, in a plan or in a review is written with its n beside it.
A break from the screen, written on the plan before the session at a fixed time, and taken whether the session is going well or badly. It is never triggered by a result.

The stretch of bars that builds a level. Prior-day levels and settlement: RTH, 09:30 to 16:00 ET. Prior-week levels: the full-session week, Sunday 18:00 to Friday 16:00 ET. Overnight levels: ETH, from 16:00 ET to the 09:30 ET open.

The official price the exchange sets for a contract. The daily settlement is set at the end of each day's settlement window; the final settlement is set once, at expiry, and is the price the contract is cashed out at.

The second tier: a named location plus the read of what price is doing there, judged on a closed bar. Price at a level either holds or fails; the read says which. It is recorded in two journal fields, the setup (the read) and the location (the slug).

Selling a contract you don't own, with the expectation that price will fall, allowing you to buy it back cheaper. You profit when price goes down. In futures, shorting is as easy as going long — no borrowing required.

The check a plan line has to pass: after the session, with only the line and the chart, you can mark the bar where it triggered and the price where it ended without guessing. A line that fails is not a plan line.

A cluster of adjacent prices inside one footprint bar, each carrying a diagonal imbalance on the same side, with bar delta running the same way. On the 5-minute footprint it is an in-session location in this course (Module 06), never a trigger.

A fast move made of triggered stop orders: price reaches a cluster of stops, they execute as market orders, and their push carries price into the next cluster. It often ends abruptly, once the stops are used up, and the move can snap back.

The smallest stop distance, in ticks, that one of your pages will accept, derived from your own adverse-excursion record for that page and session block. The stop goes behind the far edge first; if the far edge is closer than the floor, the stop goes out to the floor and size falls.

An order that triggers when price reaches a specified level, converting to a market order at that point. Used as a stop loss to limit losses when a trade goes against you. In this course the stop is set behind the zone's far edge before entry, and widening it after entry is Broke Rule.

The test of whether a price counts as a level: you can name something that already happened there (a session extreme, a volume cluster, a value edge) and a price beyond it at which the reason for the trade is gone. A stop sits behind that price. A line that fails the test is not a level.
A level a trade aims at, written before entry. It says where price may travel to; it is never a reason to enter and never a direction.

The if/then part of an idea: a named behaviour at a named level zone, the trigger that must fire there, and the level it targets. It states what you will do if price does something at a place, never where price will go.

The order every trade traces up through: the idea (what should happen, where it is wrong, and how much stands behind it), the setup (the named location and the read of what price is doing there), and the trigger (the price event at that location). Construction follows the three: level, stop, risk, size, entry. A trade missing a tier carries an honest tag, not a smaller size.
The smallest price step a contract can trade in. For MNQ and MES it is 0.25 index points, so one point is four ticks.
What one tick is worth on one contract, in dollars: tick size times the multiplier. MNQ: 0.25 × $2 = $0.50. MES: 0.25 × $5 = $1.25.
CPI, PPI, PCE, NFP, FOMC (the statement and the press conference), and Retail Sales. Be flat 5 minutes before the release; no new entries until 2 minutes after it.
Home sales, EIA, consumer sentiment, JOLTS, and Fed speakers. Stay aware of the time, manage your position through it, and never exit a working position because of it.
The journal tag for a manual exit taken for any reason other than the four. Its execution mark is Fail, whatever the trade went on to do.

The share of sessions in which price reached a line at any point in a stated window, counted from a stated start such as the open. It says nothing about the order of events, where an entry sat, or whether a stop was hit first.
The hours in which you may place a trade: 06:00 to 16:00 ET, with a focus block of 09:30 to 11:00 ET. Outside the window there is no execution of any kind.

Traders holding positions that price has just moved against, past the place they entered, such as buyers of a breakout that has fallen back inside the range. Their stops sit beyond the move, and their exit pushes price further against them. On a footprint chart this is the confirmation for the failed breakout and failed breakdown read (Modules 07 and 11).

The price event at the level that tells you to enter now, such as Pause N Go, a resting limit after displacement, or a level reclaim on a 5-minute close (Module 13). Order flow can confirm a trigger; it is never the trigger.
The named leak of trading an entry event with no level under it: a trigger fired mid-range, with nothing behind the stop. It shows in the journal as location mid-range, and the trade is No Setup.
The last few sessions of one month and the first few of the next, when month-end rebalancing and new-month flows are scheduled. Written on the calendar line as activity context, never as a direction.

The two-bar-exhaustion sub-form: a bar with large opposing delta inside it that closes near its extreme in the direction of your read, then a break of that signal bar. For a long: deep selling inside the bar, a close near its high, then a break above it.
The location name for a poor high or poor low carried onto the next session's plan. It is a target and a reason to hold toward a level; it is never an entry on its own.
A label for an entry in your own register: the rule is written and locked, and has not yet been run against data.
The upper and lower edges of the value area. The prior session's edges are the levels PD VAH and PD VAL.
A label for an entry in your own register: the rule has passed both gates, Gate 1 on market data and Gate 2 on your own live trades.
The band of prices around the POC that holds a set share of the session's volume, by convention about 70%. It is where the session did most of its business.
Vanna is how an option's hedge changes when implied volatility changes; charm is how it changes as time passes. Both make dealers trade with no move in price, and both build toward expiration.

Rule-based fund trading forced by volatility or trend: vol-control funds cut exposure as realized volatility rises and add as it falls; CTAs buy and sell when price crosses thresholds in their trend models. Both trade after the conditions change, and outside estimates of their size and thresholds are guesses.
A horizontal histogram of the volume traded at each price over a set period, usually one session. Wide rows mark prices the market accepted; thin rows mark prices it moved through or rejected.
The session's average price weighted by volume. In this course it is context, not a location: no level, stop or branch is built on it, and price above or below it is not a direction.
A label for an entry in your own register: the rule has been run and is positive, but unstable across halves or years, or rests on too few trades to read.

A setting you start from because you need one, not because a test chose it. For the footprint stacked-imbalance read, the course's working default is ratio 5 and minimum delta 15, chosen for screen clarity. You replace it with your own setting, derived from your own record.

The short list of setup, location and trigger combinations you actually take, written in the course vocabulary (TAXONOMY slugs). Only a combination on this list may become a trade. Everything else goes to the parking lot.
A level written as a price band with two edges rather than a single line. Price can trade into a zone without breaking it; acceptance through the whole zone is what changes the read.
